place.en: Foot of Mount Meng · Shi'ao village

setup.zh: 蒙山脚下的石坳村，十七户人家，一户打猎——你家。屋顶漏雨，米缸半年见底；山，是马家的。
setup.en: Shi'ao village at the foot of Mount Meng: seventeen households, one of them hunters — yours. The roof leaks, the rice jar is empty half the year; the mountain belongs to the Mas.

recap.zh: 石坳村，猎户家的孩子：爹老实，娘心细，山是马家的。
recap.en: Shi'ao village, a hunter's child: an honest father, a clever mother, and a mountain that belongs to the Mas.

zh: 十七户人家，十六户种地，一户打猎。
屋顶三年没换茅草，一下雨，盆碗齐响。
en: Shi'ao village, at the foot of Mount Meng.
Seventeen households: sixteen farm, one hunts.
Three years on the same thatch; when it rains, every bowl rings.

story.zh:
在蒙山脚下，流传着一个传说。

传说有一个少年，他的人生惨到什么地步呢？镇上的说书先生讲他的故事，讲到一半，自己先哭了，哭得收不住，只好把听众的茶钱一个一个退回去。从那以后，说书先生再也不讲这个故事了——不是不忍心，是赔不起。

这个少年，就是你。

今年十二岁。家住蒙山脚下石坳村。职业：猎户家的独子。特长：饿。

---

石坳村一共十七户人家。十六户种地，一户打猎。

打猎的那一户，就是你家。

村里人提起你家，都要竖起大拇指：「猎户家，那是祖传的手艺。」然后把大拇指收回去，补一句：「祖传的穷。」

你家有两间房。一间住人，一间挂兽皮。下雨天，两间都住水。

你娘说，咱家这屋顶，是蒙山最有学问的屋顶——它知道雨从哪来，还知道雨往哪去。

你爹说，这叫**天人合一**。

你娘说，你再合一次试试。

你爹就不说话了。他是一个很懂得什么时候不说话的人。这是他一辈子最大的本事，也是唯一的本事——哦不，还有一个：他的左膝盖。

你爹的左膝盖年轻时被野猪顶过。从此阴天疼，下雨疼，刮风疼，马家来收租之前，也疼。比村口那面铜锣还准。你爹说它是「想跟我聊聊天」。你娘说它是全家唯一一个挣不来钱、却天天有话说的。

你身上穿的衣裳，是你爹的旧衣裳改的。你爹的旧衣裳，是你爷爷的旧衣裳改的。你爷爷的旧衣裳是哪来的，没人知道。你娘算过，照这么一代一代改下去，这件衣裳的年纪，比马家的族谱还长。

说到马家——

你家最怕的，不是穷。穷你们习惯了，穷就像你爹的膝盖，天天跟你聊天，聊久了也就不当回事了。

你家最怕的，是马家。

蒙山是马家的。至少马家是这么说的。马家老爷在县衙里有个做书吏的远房表侄，于是一夜之间，满山的树姓了马，满山的兔子姓了马，满山的泉水也姓了马。村里人砍一担柴，交马家一捆；你家打一只獐子，交马家半扇。

有一年，你爹喝了二两酒，壮着胆子小声问了一句：「那山上的风，也姓马吗？」

第二天，马家就开始收「山风钱」了。

从那以后，你爹再也不喝酒了。
story.en:
At the foot of Mount Meng there is a legend.

The legend tells of a boy whose life was so miserable that — well, how miserable? When the storyteller in town told his tale, he got halfway and burst into tears himself, cried so hard he couldn't stop, and had to hand every listener back their tea money one by one. After that the storyteller never told the tale again — not because he couldn't bear to, but because he couldn't afford to.

That child is you.

You are twelve. You live in Shi'ao village at the foot of Mount Meng. Occupation: only child of the hunter's family. Special skill: being hungry.

---

Shi'ao village has seventeen households. Sixteen farm; one hunts.

The one that hunts is yours.

Whenever the villagers mention your family they give a thumbs-up: "The hunters — that's a family craft, handed down." Then they fold the thumb away and add: "Handed-down poverty."

Your family has two rooms. One for people, one for hanging hides. When it rains, water lives in both.

Your mother says this roof of ours is the most learned roof on Mount Meng — it knows where the rain comes from, and where the rain is going.

Your father says this is called **the unity of heaven and man**.

Your mother says: unite it one more time and see.

Your father stops talking. He is a man who knows exactly when to stop talking. It is the greatest skill of his life, and his only one — oh, no, there's one more: his left knee.

A wild boar gored your father's left knee when he was young. Ever since, it aches when it's cloudy, aches when it rains, aches when the wind blows, and aches right before the Mas come for the rent. More reliable than the brass gong at the village gate. Your father says the knee "just wants a chat." Your mother says it's the only member of the family who earns nothing and still has something to say every day.

The clothes you wear are your father's old clothes cut down. Your father's old clothes were your grandfather's old clothes cut down. Where your grandfather's old clothes came from, nobody knows. Your mother has worked it out: at the rate they're being cut down generation after generation, this jacket is older than the Ma family tree.

Speaking of the Mas —

What your family fears most isn't being poor. You're used to poor. Poor is like your father's knee: it chats with you every day, and after long enough you stop paying it any mind.

What your family fears most is the Mas.

Mount Meng belongs to the Mas. That's what the Mas say, anyway. Old Master Ma has a distant nephew who clerks at the county yamen, and so overnight every tree on the mountain took the name Ma, every hare on the mountain took the name Ma, and every spring on the mountain took the name Ma too. A villager cuts a load of firewood, a bundle goes to the Mas; your family takes a river deer, half of it goes to the Mas.

One year your father had two taels of wine, worked up his nerve and asked, very quietly: "The wind on the mountain — is its name Ma too?"

The next day the Mas started collecting "mountain wind money."

Your father has not touched wine since.
